verdicts.trueWording: no college of heralds for enforcement
verdicts.note: Raw wayback capture of the SSM entry (13 Apr 1999) read in full. Para 1: 'the rules of heraldry are a good deal more flexible in the Seven Kingdoms... There are no "laws" of heraldry per se, no college of heralds for enforcement, no formal regulations about cadency and differencing.' Quote verbatim; Seven Kingdoms limb explicit in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: individual knights and lords have a certain amount of freedom
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'So individual knights and lords have a certain amount of freedom to bear what shields they prefer and play around with their house sigils... or not, as the case may be.' Quote verbatim; the Westeros limb carries from the Seven Kingdoms framing of the preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: Ser Garlan (the second son) with two roses on his shield
verdicts.note: Page: 'All three sons of Mace Tyrell are entitled to bear the Highgarden rose... but when two or more of them are fighting together on the same field, you will often see Ser Garlan (the second son) with two roses on his shield, and Ser Loras (the thirdborn) with three.' Quote verbatim; second-son, two-roses and same-field limbs all present, and 'differencing' is the entry's own vocabulary ('no formal regulations about cadency and differencing').

verdicts.trueWording: quarter the arms of their mother's and grandmother's houses
verdicts.note: Page: 'Thus Big and Little Walder, at Winterfell, quarter the arms of their mother's and grandmother's houses on their shields and surcoats, though they could just as lawfully wear the Frey towers unadorned.' Quote verbatim (page uses typographic apostrophes); shields-and-surcoats and lawful-unadorned-towers limbs both present.

verdicts.trueWording: heraldry was unregulated and very much a matter of individual choice
verdicts.note: Final paragraph, as the page hint says: 'This sort of stuff happened all the time in the Dark Ages and early Middle Ages, where heraldry was unregulated and very much a matter of individual choice. It was only later that everything became formalized.' Quote verbatim; the grounding limb is the sentence's own 'this sort of stuff' back-reference to the Westerosi examples.

verdicts.trueWording: though I haven't yet decided what they were
verdicts.note: Second paragraph, as the page hint says: 'Some of the old Kings in the North also had their own personal variants, undoubtedly, though I haven't yet decided what they were.' Quote verbatim; 'undoubtedly' and the undecided limb both present, and the paragraph's subject (Robb's wolf's-head shield vs the running-wolf banner) makes 'variants' heraldic.

verdicts.trueWording: he's a great writer, period, and deserves a place in the canon
verdicts.note: Live georgerrmartin.com post fetched raw (dated July 17, 2009). Body paragraph 2: 'Vance is not only a great SF and fantasy writer, he's a great writer, period, and deserves a place in the canon of American literature.' Quote verbatim; both limbs in one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: [Vance] had a huge influence on me and my work
verdicts.note: Live harpervoyagerbooks.co.uk post fetched raw; embedded JSON-LD datePublished 2013-06-03, matching the citation. Pull-quote opens '[Vance] had a huge influence on me and my work, and for the past fifty-some years has ranked among my very favorite writers.' Quote verbatim; the relaying limb is confirmed by the lead-in, 'posted a moving tribute to Jack Vance on his Not a Blog last week', and the '- George R. R. Martin' attribution.

verdicts.trueWording: France's best historical novelist since Dumas Pere
verdicts.note: Live georgerrmartin.com page fetched raw (March 30, 2013). Final body paragraph: '...you won't go wrong with Maurice Druon, France's best historical novelist since Dumas Pere.' Quote verbatim, in the final paragraph as the page hint says.

verdicts.trueWording: a technique writers like Martin use with great success
verdicts.note: Live reactormag.com review fetched raw (Stefan Raets, March 12, 2013). Narrative-voice paragraph: 'Sure, The Iron King switches perspective from chapter to chapter, a technique writers like Martin use with great success to show complex intrigues from various points of view.' Quote verbatim; Martin is named inside the praised class, and the 'complex intrigues from various points of view' limb is the same sentence's tail.

verdicts.trueWording: occasionally uses an ominous-sounding omniscient narrator
verdicts.note: Same paragraph: 'What's more jarring is that The Iron King occasionally uses an ominous-sounding omniscient narrator ("But new events were on their way which would change the destinies of them all."), and this immediately makes it sound more dated.' Quote verbatim; the 'immediately... more dated' limb is the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: sometimes by the territory they control
verdicts.note: Characters paragraph, as the page hint says: 'A few of them are sometimes referred to by name, sometimes by title, and sometimes by the territory they control, which may have you paging back to the list of the characters at the front of the book to double-check who is who more than a few times.' Quote verbatim; the name/title/territory triple and the send-back-to-the-character-list limb are both present ('A few of them' matches the claim's 'some characters').

verdicts.trueWording: explain past events to people who don't need them explained
verdicts.note: Narrative-voice paragraph: 'The occasional tendency of characters to explain past events to people who don't need them explained has the same effect:' - 'the same effect' referring to the immediately preceding 'makes it sound more dated', so the dated limb is supported anaphorically rather than by a restated phrase; quote itself verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: the Starks and the Lannisters have nothing on the Capets
verdicts.note: Final paragraph of the review: 'as Martin says in the Foreword, "the Starks and the Lannisters have nothing on the Capets and the Plantagenets."' Quote verbatim. Foreword limb explicit; the 2013 HarperCollins-edition limb is supported by the review's closing line, 'The Iron King is published by HarperCollins UK. It is available March 26', on a page published March 12, 2013.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin doesn't engage in one-to-one associations
verdicts.note: Live reactormag.com article fetched raw (Michael Livingston, July 16, 2015). Wars of the Roses paragraph, as the page hint says: 'But it's hardly as simple as a math equation: Martin's Starks and Baratheons don't equal the historical Yorks... Martin doesn't engage in one-to-one associations between the real world and his fictional one.' Quote verbatim; the medievalist limb is supported by the byline note ('Professor of Medieval Literature at The Citadel') and the opening 'my fellow medievalists'.
